evidence: The resolution is capacity/scheduling — additional hosts, chunked prefill, admission control/backpressure, or P/D disaggregation. ... Hosts were raised from H=1 to H=21. That is the capacity floor, which is the max of the named screens, not the prefill compute screen alone: case (i)’s prefill screen needs ⌈18.6⌉ = 19 hosts, but the KV-residency / Little’s-Law screen needs ⌈344/17⌉ = 21 hosts at the peak and therefore binds (Ch 8 §3; Ch 17).
issue: The mini-case resolution says the host count was raised to H = 21, but the chapter has not established that the described deployment actually has the 17 KV slots per host used by the Little’s-Law screen. The chapter’s own running case starts from a single host and diagnoses a prefill oversubscription; jumping to H = 21 by importing the canonical 17-slot screen is a cross-scenario substitution. The text presents H = 21 as the resolution of this mini-case, but the canonical 17-slot figure belongs to the 9.5K-token resident-basis geometry, not necessarily to the mini-case’s named deployment. This is a scope/referent ambiguity: the reader cannot tell whether 21 hosts is the answer for the mini-case or merely the canonical workload’s separate screen.
fix_instruction: State explicitly that the mini-case adopts the canonical 9.5K-token resident-basis host geometry and the same 17-slot KV screen; otherwise recompute the KV slot count for the mini-case’s actual resident token count and context distribution before quoting H = 21. Add one sentence separating the mini-case’s measured/inferred host count from the canonical Ch 17 screen.

evidence: The raised ceiling also survives this chapter’s binding per-rank test: per-rank weights are 39.24375 ÷ 8 = 4.906 GB, leaving 80 − 4.906 − 8 = 67.09 GB of KV budget per rank, which holds 67.09 ÷ 3.11296 = 21.55 → floor 21 sequences — the same integer the aggregate division gives, so the ceiling is not an aggregate artifact.
issue: The per-rank arithmetic silently changes the reserve basis. The aggregate calculation subtracts a fixed 64 GB host reserve (640 − 39.24375 − 64 = 536.75625 GB). The per-rank calculation subtracts 8 GB per rank, which is the 64 GB host reserve divided by 8. That is internally consistent, but the prose calls 8 GB “the full runtime-reserve share” without repeating that it is a host-level reserve divided across ranks. Because the preceding sentence says “per-rank weights are 39.24375 ÷ 8 = 4.906 GB, leaving 80 − 4.906 − 8 = 67.09 GB,” a reader can easily read the 8 GB as a per-rank measured reserve rather than as 64/8. The quantity has two possible meanings and the text does not disambiguate at the point of use.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the per-rank sentence to say “the 64 GB host reserve divided by 8 ranks = 8 GB per rank” and label it as the same planning reserve, not a measured per-rank allocation. Keep the aggregate and per-rank reserve definitions adjacent so the 8 GB cannot be mistaken for an independent per-rank constant.

evidence: The ~11.1 GFLOP delta is arithmetic on Table 5‑1’s model-card rows, so it is [1P][DERIVED]; the open claim that remains [1P][HYPOTHESIS] is the separate one about whether the ~15% MAP uplift transfers to the target corpus.
issue: The sentence labels the open transfer claim as [1P][HYPOTHESIS], but the preceding text explicitly says the ~15% MAP uplift is an [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] scenario input, not a first-party fact. Calling the transfer claim [1P][HYPOTHESIS] mixes provenance: the hypothesis is about an illustrative assumption, not about a first-party model-card value. This is a label/provenance mismatch that can mislead a reader into thinking the 15% figure has first-party provenance.
fix_instruction: Change the label on the transfer claim to [ILLUSTRATIVE][HYPOTHESIS] (or otherwise state that the hypothesis concerns the [ILLUSTRATIVE][ASSUMPTION] uplift), reserving [1P] for the model-card parameter and dimension rows only.

evidence: Current-gen models commonly ship windows ranging from roughly 8K tokens in older or small-tier deployments up to a million-plus tokens at the frontier, varying by model and vendor — for example, the Qwen3.8-Flash-Next card states a native 262K-token window with YaRN extension to 1M, and the GLM-5.3-Flash and DeepSeek-V4 cards state 1M ([1P][FACT] model cards: HF Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next; HF zai-org/GLM-5.3-Flash; DeepSeek-V4 technical report, arXiv 2606.19348, and model card HF deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro — all accessed 2026-08-30, the book’s evidence cutoff; Appendix A §10); the low end of that range is the older/edge tier rather than a published figure for a current frontier model — this book’s reading of the vendor line-ups above, not a vendor statement [1P][HYPOTHESIS].
issue: The sentence begins by saying current-gen models commonly ship windows “ranging from roughly 8K tokens in older or small-tier deployments up to a million-plus tokens at the frontier,” then admits the low end is “the older/edge tier rather than a published figure for a current frontier model.” That is a scope drift: the opening claim is about current-gen models, while the cited support covers only the high end. A reader can reasonably infer that current frontier models still commonly ship 8K windows, which the sentence itself later disclaims.
fix_instruction: Rewrite the opening clause to separate the historical/edge tier from the current frontier tier: e.g. “Older or small-tier deployments may still ship roughly 8K-token windows, while current frontier cards commonly advertise hundreds of thousands to a million-plus tokens.” Keep the cited Qwen/GLM/DeepSeek examples attached only to the frontier claim.

evidence: The p99 position is 1 + (N−1) × 0.99 = 9,900.01. The sorted-sample ranks are 9,900 → 1.30 s and 9,901 → 5.0 s, so 1.30 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.30) ≈ 1.33 s: the interpolation lands just past the largest non-straggler draw, between it and the first straggler.
issue: The interpolation explanation says the p99 position is 9,900.01, but the sorted-sample ranks used are 9,900 and 9,901. With the standard percentile interpolation formula, the fractional part of the 1-based rank should be applied between rank 9,900 and rank 9,901, so the interpolation fraction is 0.01, not 0.01 of the difference between those ranks? Actually the arithmetic is correct: 1.30 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.30) = 1.337. The wording “lands just past the largest non-straggler draw” is the real issue: it implies the largest non-straggler is at rank 9,900, but the interpolation is between the 9,900th and 9,901st sorted values; the text does not state what the 9,900th value is or whether it is the largest non-straggler. This is a minor clarity issue, not an arithmetic error.
fix_instruction: State the sorted values explicitly: “rank 9,900 = 1.30 s, rank 9,901 = 5.0 s; the interpolated p99 is 1.30 + 0.01 × (5.0 − 1.30) = 1.337 s.” Avoid the phrase “largest non-straggler draw” unless the rank-9,900 value is identified as such.
